correctness.rationale: For the unit regular tetrahedral surface, the last-edge-entry bound proves globally that opposite-face geodesic distance is the minimum of three unfolded-source distances. Their Voronoi cells give three disjoint distance-preserving convex kites with radial boundary sec(π/6−|θ|). Exact integration and normalization by area sqrt(3) establish the full CDF, density, moment integral, exact first two moments, 3/2 cusp and quadratic endpoint tail. Finite Monte Carlo, adaptive quadrature and high-precision asymptotic checks succeeded but are not the proof.

originality.rationale: The claimed object is the entire exact surface-area law of shortest path distance from a fixed vertex of a unit regular tetrahedron. Searches and material inspection found generic cut-locus/source-unfolding results, classifications of tetrahedral geodesics, and planar distance-distribution methods, but no equivalent normalized CDF and moment/singularity identities; the known results supply methods, not the evaluated invariant. The result may be algorithmically derivable from broader tools and historical priority remains provisional.
residual_risks: An earlier unindexed educational or historical computation could already give the same tetrahedron intrinsic radial law.

The CDF is computationally accessible by combining general polyhedral source unfolding with planar triangle integration; the precise specialized closed form and singularities, rather than new machinery, are the assessed contribution.

The 2005 tetrahedron intersection/chord paper and 2007 closed-geodesics paper were compared at bibliographic/abstract level only because their stated metrics and questions differ; no full-text noncoverage assertion is made for them.
Independent historical-priority verification has not been performed.

value.rationale: The exact metric-ball area profile at a tetrahedral vertex is a natural, previously unevaluated intrinsic metric-measure invariant. The complete law identifies the onset of wavefront overlap at the non-source vertices, a sharp 3/2-power area deficit, a quadratic terminal tail and all distance moments. It is an analytical benchmark for algorithms computing geodesic distances on polyhedral surfaces, rather than an arbitrary parameter or numerical experiment.
